new_en: The laws of rolling a Sefer Torah. It contains 8 seifim: It is forbidden to hold a bare Sefer Torah without a cloth. {Rama: Some say that the same law applies to other sacred writings. [Agudah and Tosafos, chapter 1 of Shabbos] This is not the custom, but it is proper to be stringent if one has not washed his hands. Regarding a Sefer Torah, even in such a case it is forbidden. [Rama's own ruling; Agudah]} The greatest among those who read from the Torah performs the rolling, and the custom is to purchase this honor for a high price in order to endear the mitzvah. {Rama: Some say that if the mantle is linen on 1 side and silk on the other, the silk side should be turned toward the Sefer Torah when it is rolled. [Mordechai, end of Megillah] This is not the custom. [Beit Yosef, siman 123] One should not roll the Sefer Torah with a torn cloth if another is available. [Maharil] One should not make coverings for a Sefer Torah from old items that were previously used for an ordinary purpose. See above, siman 153. [Agudah, Menachos; Responsa Maharil, siman 114; Beit Yosef; Rashbatz]}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: The laws of joining for a zimun of 3 or 10. It contains 4 seifim: If 2 people ate together and finished, and a third person arrived, whenever they could still eat something were it brought to them, he joins with them, and they are obligated to give him food so that he can join them. This applies only if he arrived before they said, 'Bring us so that we may bless.' But if they already said, 'Bring us so that we may bless,' and afterward the third person arrived, he does not join them. {Rama: Washing mayim acharonim has the same status as saying, 'Bring us so that we may bless.' [Mordechai, chapter 3, Sheloshah SheAchlu] See above, siman 179.}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: The laws of error and doubt in the blessing over wine. It contains 3 seifim: If one took a cup of beer or water and began, 'Blessed are You, Hashem our God, King of the universe,' intending to conclude SheHakol, but erred and concluded Borei Pri HaGafen, we do not require him to repeat the blessing, because when he mentioned the Divine Name and kingship, which are the essence of the blessing, he intended the blessing appropriate to that species. Some say that if he took a cup of beer or water thinking it was wine, began, 'Blessed are You, Hashem our God, King of the universe,' intending to say Borei Pri HaGafen, then remembered that it was beer or water and concluded SheHakol, he has fulfilled his obligation. {Rama: All the more so, if he had wine in his hand and thought it was water, began intending to say SheHakol, then remembered and recited Borei Pri HaGafen, he has fulfilled his obligation, since even had he concluded SheHakol he would have fulfilled his obligation. [Tur]}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: Answering Amen after blessings. It contains 4 seifim: One does not answer Amen after his own blessings except after 2 or more blessings that conclude a series of blessings. The custom is to answer Amen after Yehalelucha and after Yishtabach. {Rama: Some say that one answers Amen only after the blessing Boneh Yerushalayim in Birkat HaMazon, and this is the widespread custom in these countries and should not be changed. [Tosafos and Mordechai, beginning of chapter Sheloshah SheAchlu; Maharik, shoresh 72]} In places where the custom is to answer Amen after Yehalelucha and Yishtabach, one should also answer Amen after the blessing Shomer Amo Yisrael La'ad.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: Who lights the Shabbos lamps and the law when one erred on a cloudy day. It contains 17 seifim: One should be careful to prepare a fine lamp. Some intend to use 2 wicks, 1 corresponding to Zachor and 1 corresponding to Shamor. {Rama: One may add and kindle 3 or 4 lamps, and this is the custom. A woman who once forgot to kindle lights 3 lamps for the rest of her life. [Maharil] One may add to a number that corresponds to another concept, provided that one does not reduce it. [Ashiri and Mordechai, Rosh Hashana, beginning of chapter Yom Tov]}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: In a place where wine is not commonly available, some say that Kiddush may be recited over beer and other beverages, except water; others say that Kiddush may not be recited over them. According to the Rosh, at night one should not recite Kiddush over beer but rather over bread. In the morning it is preferable to recite Kiddush over beer so that he will recite SheHakol before HaMotzi, because if he first recites Kiddush over bread there is no recognizable change from an ordinary meal. These are reasonable words. {Rama: The widespread custom follows the Rosh. If wine is available in the city, he should not recite Kiddush over bread. One who does not drink wine because of a vow may recite Kiddush over wine and have the others reclining with him drink it. If no others are with him, he should recite Kiddush over bread rather than wine, or hear Kiddush from others. [Hagahot Maimoniyot, chapter 29; Responsa Maimoniyot, Sefer Hafla'ah, siman 4]}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: That one should not bow at 'U'lecha anachnu modim.' It contains 1 seif: One should not bow at 'U'lecha anachnu modim,' because one may bow only in the places established by the Sages. {Rama: The custom on Shabbos is to come to the synagogue later than on weekdays, because regarding the weekday tamid it says 'in the morning,' while regarding Shabbos it says 'and on the Shabbos day,' which implies delay. [Mordechai, end of chapter 22] The custom is also to increase the Shabbos zemirot, each place according to its custom. If any of them were omitted, one does not return, except that if he omitted 'LaKel asher shavat,' etc., he returns. One may prolong and beautify the zemirot, and one should not protest against a person who prolongs them even if the protest is motivated by concern for bitul Torah. [Or Zarua] Nevertheless, on Shabbos and Yom Tov one should not prolong them excessively, so that they eat before the sixth hour, as stated below in siman 288.}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: Which activities may be discussed on Shabbos. It contains 14 seifim: From the verse 'from pursuing your affairs,' we learn that one's affairs are forbidden even when no melacha is being performed, such as inspecting one's property to determine what will be needed tomorrow, or walking to the entrance of the city in order to hurry out at night to the bathhouse. Likewise, one may not wait at the techum boundary toward nightfall in order to hire workers. But one may wait there in order to bring his animal. Some say that if the animal cannot walk on its own legs, such as a small lamb, he may not wait there, because he may not bring it, since it is forbidden to move an animal, which is muktzeh. {Rama: Likewise, it is forbidden to stroll about in order to find a horse, ship, or wagon with which to depart after Shabbos. [Mordechai, end of chapter Mi SheHechshich]}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: The laws of Shabbos that depend upon speech. It contains 22 seifim: 'And speak a matter' teaches that one's speech on Shabbos should not be like one's speech on a weekday. Therefore it is forbidden to say, 'I will do such-and-such tomorrow,' or, 'I will purchase such-and-such merchandise tomorrow.' Even idle conversation should not be excessive. {Rama: For people who derive enjoyment from relating reports and new matters, it is permitted to discuss them on Shabbos as on a weekday. But one who does not enjoy such conversation may not say these things merely so that his fellow will enjoy them. [Terumat HaDeshen, siman 61]}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: The law of tying and making bows on Shabbos. It contains 7 seifim: One who ties a permanent knot that is a craftsman's knot is liable, such as camel drivers' knots, sailors' knots, and the knots in shoe and sandal straps that shoemakers tie when making them, and all similar knots. One who ties a permanent knot that is not a craftsman's knot is exempt from liability. {Rama: Some disagree and hold that one is liable for every permanent knot, even a layman's knot. [Rashi, Rosh, Rabbeinu Yeruham, and Tur] Some say that any knot that one does not intend to open that same day is called permanent. [Kol Bo and others] Others are lenient and hold that a knot intended for less than 7 days is not called permanent. [Tur and Mordechai]} It is permitted initially to tie a knot that is neither permanent nor a craftsman's knot. {Rama: The law of untying is the same as the law of tying. [Tur]} Thus, if one's strap tore and he tied it, a rope snapped and he tied it, he tied a rope to a bucket, or he tied an animal's rein, he is exempt; the same applies to all simple knots intended to remain. A craftsman's knot tied temporarily is forbidden, though one is not liable. It is permitted to tie a temporary knot for a mitzvah purpose, such as in order to measure a required halachic measure. See above, siman 314. {Rama: Some say that one should not untie any double knot, because we are not certain what constitutes a craftsman's knot. Even when intended only temporarily, such a knot may not be tied or untied, and this is the custom. [Hagahot Alfasi] Nevertheless, where it causes distress it may be untied, since the prohibition is rabbinic and the Sages did not impose it in a case of distress. This law of a double knot concerns tying 2 ends together; but making a single knot in the same cord or thread is treated like a double knot. [Semag]}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.

new_en: The laws of borrowing and acquiring Shabbos needs, rinsing utensils, repairing them, and immersing them on Shabbos. It contains 10 seifim: One may say to another person, 'Fill this vessel for me,' even if the vessel is specifically designated as a measure. This applies when the purchaser takes the seller's measuring vessel and carries it home, and certainly when the purchaser brings a vessel from his own home and says, 'Fill this vessel for me.' But it is forbidden to measure with a vessel specifically designated for measuring and then pour the contents into the purchaser's vessels. {Rama: Some are lenient whenever he does not intend an exact measure, but reduces or adds a little. [Hagahot Ashiri and Mordechai, chapter Ein Tzedin] The widespread custom therefore is to measure with a vessel designated for measuring and pour it into the purchaser's vessels. The reason for those who are lenient will be explained immediately below. The law of a Shabbos loan is the same as on Yom Tov; see above, siman 525, and above, siman 307, seif 11.}
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; Rama gloss restored in source order.
